evidence.excerpt: Optimal pricing functions derived from queueing or simulation models are computationally expensive to evaluate in real time, limiting their use in shop-floor execution systems. This paper investigates whether gradient-boosted regression trees trained on offline simulation data can serve as fast surrogates for a six-machine, ten-job-class job shop pricing model. A training dataset of 120,000 state-action-reward triples is generated from AnyLogic simulations. The trained surrogate predicts the near-optimal price for a new arriving job within 2 milliseconds on standard hardware, compared with 40 seconds for direct simulation lookahead. In a rolling-horizon production test, the surrogate policy achieves 97.4% of the revenue attained by the full simulation-based policy. Feature importance analysis identifies current aggregate utilisation and job processing time as the two most influential inputs, with job class contributing less than expected. The paper discusses data requirements and retraining frequency for production deployment.
